question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
I used to eat into / in the evening / when my parents / were on night shifts.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. I used to eat into.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "I used to eat into / in the evening / when my parents / were on night shifts."

• The phrasal verb "eat into" means to gradually destroy, corrode, wear away, or use up something (e.g., "Rust eats into metal"; "The fine ate into his savings"). It does NOT simply mean "to have a meal".

• Since the sentence merely describes the habitual act of having a meal in the evening, the preposition "into" should not follow "eat" at all — the correct segment is simply "I used to eat...".

• Corrected sentence: "I used to eat in the evening when my parents were on night shifts."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "when my parents" is grammatically correct; it correctly introduces the subordinate clause of time.

• Option 3: "in the evening" is grammatically correct; it is a correct adverbial phrase of time.

• Option 4: "were on night shifts" is grammatically correct; the past tense verb "were" correctly agrees with the plural subject "my parents".

NOTE

• "Eat into" = to use up or destroy something gradually, e.g., "Medical bills ate into his savings."

• Other commonly tested phrasal verbs with "eat": "eat away (at)" (to gradually erode/destroy), "eat up" (to consume completely), "eat out" (to have a meal at a restaurant).

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
(1) Ganga was (2) out shopping at the mall (3) and ran over (4) her schoolmate.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. segment (3) "and ran over".

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "(1) Ganga was (2) out shopping at the mall (3) and ran over (4) her schoolmate."

• The phrasal verb "run over" means to hit and drive a vehicle over a person or animal, causing injury or death — it does not mean "to meet someone by chance".

• The intended meaning of the sentence is that Ganga unexpectedly met/encountered her schoolmate while out shopping. The correct phrasal verb for this meaning is "run into" (to meet unexpectedly), not "run over".

• Corrected sentence: "Ganga was out shopping at the mall and ran into her schoolmate."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 (segment 3).

Additional Information

• Option 1 (segment 4 – "her schoolmate") is incorrect because this segment is grammatically fine; it is simply the object noun phrase.

• Option 2 (segment 1 – "Ganga was") is incorrect because this segment is grammatically fine; correct subject with the past tense auxiliary "was".

• Option 3 (segment 2 – "out shopping at the mall") is incorrect because this segment is grammatically fine; a correct adverbial phrase describing what Ganga was doing.

NOTE

• "Run into" = to meet someone unexpectedly; also, to collide with something.

• "Run over" = to hit and drive a vehicle over someone/something.

• "Run through" = to rehearse or review quickly; also, to pierce with a weapon.

• "Run out of" = to have no more of something left.

question:
The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains an error.
Shall have / you bring / your note-book / tomorrow?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Shall have.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "Shall have / you bring / your note-book / tomorrow?"

• Rule — Interrogative form of the Simple Future Tense: Shall/Will + Subject + V1 + Object + ?. No form of "have" is used in this structure.

• The segment "Shall have" wrongly inserts the auxiliary "have", which belongs to the Perfect tenses, not the Simple Future. The correct opening is simply "Shall".

• Corrected sentence: "Shall you bring your note-book tomorrow?"

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "you bring" is grammatically correct; correct subject and base-form verb for the future interrogative.

• Option 3: "tomorrow" is grammatically correct; a correct adverb of time consistent with the future tense.

• Option 4: "your note-book" is grammatically correct; a correct object noun phrase.

NOTE

• Do not confuse the Simple Future interrogative (Shall/Will + Subject + V1...?) with the Future Perfect interrogative (Shall/Will + Subject + have + V3...?), e.g., "Shall you have finished your work by tomorrow?"

• "Shall" is traditionally used with "I/We" for simple future and is also used in formal questions to ask about someone else's intention, as here with "you".

question: Select the option with the correct use of future tense.
option_1: If you worked hard in the same manner, you will soon achieve success.
option_2: If you had work hard in the same manner, you will soon achieve success.
option_3: If you have work hard in the same manner, you will soon achieve success.
option_4: If you work hard in the same manner, you will soon achieve success.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. If you work hard in the same manner, you will soon achieve success.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• This is a First Conditional sentence, used to talk about a real and likely condition in the future and its probable result.

• Rule — First Conditional: If + Subject + V1/V5 (Simple Present) ..., Subject + will + V1 (Simple Future).

• Applying the rule: the "if"-clause must be in the Simple Present Tense — "If you work hard..." — and the main clause correctly uses the Simple Future — "...you will soon achieve success."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "worked" (Simple Past) is used in the if-clause instead of the required Simple Present "work".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "had work" is not a valid verb form at all; it wrongly mixes the Past Perfect auxiliary "had" with the base form "work".

• Option 3 is incorrect because "have work" is not a valid verb form; "have" would require a past participle ("have worked"), not the base form "work".

NOTE

• Second Conditional (unreal/hypothetical present): If + Subject + V2, Subject + would + V1. e.g., "If you worked hard, you would achieve success."

• Third Conditional (unreal past): If + Subject + had + V3, Subject + would have + V3. e.g., "If you had worked hard, you would have achieved success."

• The if-clause of the First Conditional never uses "will", even though it refers to the future.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been left out. Select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In todays fast-paced and technology-driven world, (1) ________ is crucial to disconnect occasionally for the sake of our health. (2) __________exposure to screens and the demands of the digital era can lead to stress, anxiety and reduced well-being. Taking time to unplug and engage (3) _____________activities that promote relaxation, such as spending time in nature, (4) _______hobbies or simply enjoying quality time with loved ones allows us to recharge, find balance and (5) __________our mental and physical health.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. it.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires the impersonal/dummy pronoun "it", used as a grammatical subject before an adjective + to-infinitive construction.

• Rule: "It + is/was + adjective + to-infinitive" is the standard structure used to state that something (expressed later by the infinitive) is important/necessary/crucial, e.g., "It is crucial to disconnect occasionally."

• Here, "it" stands for the general act of disconnecting, which is described afterwards by "to disconnect occasionally for the sake of our health".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "that" is incorrect because "that" is a demonstrative/relative pronoun that needs a specific, already-mentioned antecedent; there is none here.

• Option 2: "this" is incorrect for the same reason as "that" — it is a demonstrative pronoun pointing to something specific already stated, which is absent here.

• Option 3: "these" is incorrect because it is a plural demonstrative pronoun and would not agree with the singular verb "is" that follows.

NOTE

• Common exam pattern: "It is + adjective (necessary/important/crucial/advisable) + to + V1", e.g., "It is important to stay hydrated."

• Do not confuse this impersonal "it" with the demonstrative "it" that refers back to a specific noun already mentioned in the sentence.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been left out. Select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In todays fast-paced and technology-driven world, (1) ________ is crucial to disconnect occasionally for the sake of our health. (2) __________exposure to screens and the demands of the digital era can lead to stress, anxiety and reduced well-being. Taking time to unplug and engage (3) _____________activities that promote relaxation, such as spending time in nature, (4) _______hobbies or simply enjoying quality time with loved ones allows us to recharge, find balance and (5) __________our mental and physical health.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Constant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank describes exposure to screens that "can lead to stress, anxiety and reduced well-being" — this negative outcome is best explained by continuous, unbroken exposure, i.e., "Constant exposure".

• "Constant" means happening all the time or repeatedly, without stopping — this matches the idea of prolonged, unrelieved screen use causing harm.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Interrupted" is incorrect because it means broken off/discontinued, which contradicts the sense of persistent exposure needed here.

• Option 2: "Sporadic" is incorrect because it means occurring only occasionally or at irregular intervals, which would not typically be described as leading to stress and anxiety.

• Option 4: "Redundant" is incorrect because it means superfluous/no longer needed, which does not fit the context of screen exposure at all.

NOTE

• Words of continuity often tested together: constant, continuous, incessant, perpetual, unremitting.

• Words of irregularity often tested together: sporadic, intermittent, occasional, fitful.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been left out. Select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In todays fast-paced and technology-driven world, (1) ________ is crucial to disconnect occasionally for the sake of our health. (2) __________exposure to screens and the demands of the digital era can lead to stress, anxiety and reduced well-being. Taking time to unplug and engage (3) _____________activities that promote relaxation, such as spending time in nature, (4) _______hobbies or simply enjoying quality time with loved ones allows us to recharge, find balance and (5) __________our mental and physical health.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. in.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Fixed Preposition: the verb "engage", when it means to participate or take part in something, is always followed by the preposition "in" — "engage in (an activity)".

• Applying the rule: "...engage in activities that promote relaxation..." is the grammatically correct collocation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "into" is incorrect; "engage into" is not a standard English collocation.

• Option 3: "to" is incorrect; "engage to" changes the meaning (e.g., "engaged to be married") and does not fit here.

• Option 4: "for" is incorrect; "engage for" is not the correct preposition for this sense of "engage".

NOTE

• Other verbs commonly tested with fixed prepositions: indulge in, participate in, believe in, rejoice in, persist in.

• Do not confuse "engage in" (to participate in) with "engage with" (to interact meaningfully with someone/something) or "engage to" (to promise to marry).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been left out. Select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In todays fast-paced and technology-driven world, (1) ________ is crucial to disconnect occasionally for the sake of our health. (2) __________exposure to screens and the demands of the digital era can lead to stress, anxiety and reduced well-being. Taking time to unplug and engage (3) _____________activities that promote relaxation, such as spending time in nature, (4) _______hobbies or simply enjoying quality time with loved ones allows us to recharge, find balance and (5) __________our mental and physical health.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. pursuing.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Pursuing hobbies" is the standard, natural collocation used to describe engaging in a leisure activity for enjoyment, in the same sense as "spending time in nature" earlier in the list.

• "Pursue" here means to carry on or devote oneself to (an activity) over time, which correctly fits "hobbies".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "constructing" is incorrect; one does not "construct" a hobby — this collocation does not exist in this sense.

• Option 3: "chasing" is incorrect; "chasing hobbies" is not an idiomatic English collocation (one may "chase a dream" but not "chase hobbies").

• Option 4: "trailing" is incorrect; "trailing" means following behind something/someone, which does not fit with "hobbies".

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with hobbies/interests: pursue a hobby, take up a hobby, indulge in a hobby, cultivate an interest.

• "Pursue" is also commonly tested in phrases like "pursue a career", "pursue an education" and "pursue happiness".

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been left out. Select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

In todays fast-paced and technology-driven world, (1) ________ is crucial to disconnect occasionally for the sake of our health. (2) __________exposure to screens and the demands of the digital era can lead to stress, anxiety and reduced well-being. Taking time to unplug and engage (3) _____________activities that promote relaxation, such as spending time in nature, (4) _______hobbies or simply enjoying quality time with loved ones allows us to recharge, find balance and (5) __________our mental and physical health.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank no. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. prioritise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...allows us to recharge, find balance and prioritise our mental and physical health."

• "Prioritise" means to treat something as more important than other things, and it is a transitive verb that directly takes an object ("our mental and physical health") without needing a preposition — exactly matching the sentence structure.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "precede" is incorrect; it means to come before something in time or order, which does not make sense with "our mental and physical health" as an object here.

• Option 2: "focus" is incorrect on its own because "focus" is normally used with the preposition "on" ("focus on our health"); used without "on" it does not fit the sentence grammatically.

• Option 4: "underscore" is incorrect; it means to emphasize or highlight a fact/point, which does not fit the idea of actively taking care of one's health.

NOTE

• "Prioritise" (British spelling) / "prioritize" (American spelling) — both forms are accepted in most exams.

• Commonly confused with "focus on", which requires the preposition "on" before its object, unlike "prioritise", which does not.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
I don't like dirty cars, so you should keep it ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. spotless.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Spotless" means completely clean, without any dirt or stains — this directly answers the speaker's dislike of "dirty cars" and fits logically with keeping the car clean.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "shabby" is incorrect because it means worn out or in poor condition/untidy, which contradicts the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "similar" is incorrect because it means alike/resembling something else, which is unrelated to cleanliness.

• Option 3: "new" is incorrect because being "new" does not necessarily mean being clean, and it does not logically follow from disliking dirty cars.

NOTE

• Words related to cleanliness often tested together: spotless, immaculate, pristine, spick and span.

• Words related to dirtiness: grimy, filthy, soiled, unkempt.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to complete the given sentence.
With the increasing market prices and stagnant salaries, he is _________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. feeling the pinch.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "feeling the pinch" means to experience financial hardship, especially due to having less money than before. (आर्थिक तंगी महसूस करना)
◦ Example: With fuel prices rising every week, most families are feeling the pinch.

• With rising market prices and salaries staying the same, a person's real income effectively falls, causing financial strain — exactly the sense conveyed by "feeling the pinch".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To take a break (आराम करना): To pause or rest from an activity for a while — unrelated to financial difficulty.

• Option 3: To beat the rap (सज़ा से बच निकलना): To escape punishment or the consequences of wrongdoing.

• Option 4: To get something off one's chest (मन की बात कहकर हल्का होना): To speak openly about something that has been worrying or bothering one for a long time.

NOTE

• Other money/hardship related idioms often asked in SSC: "to make ends meet" (to have just enough money to live on), "to be in the red" (to be in debt), "to tighten one's belt" (to spend less money than before).

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Stoic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Fervent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Stoic" means a person who is able to endure hardship, pain, or difficulty without showing their feelings or complaining; impassive and unemotional. (धैर्यवान/भावनाओं को न दिखाने वाला)

• "Fervent" means showing intense and passionate feeling; full of ardour or emotion, which is the direct opposite of remaining calm and unemotional like a stoic person. (उत्कट/जोशीला)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Tolerant" (सहनशील): Able to accept views/behaviour one may not agree with — not truly opposite to "stoic"; in fact somewhat close to it.

• Option 2: "Apathetic" (उदासीन): Showing little or no interest/concern — this is close in meaning to "stoic" (unemotional), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "Cooperative" (सहयोगी): Willing to help/work with others — unrelated to the emotional-expression sense of "stoic".

NOTE

• Synonyms of "stoic": impassive, unemotional, phlegmatic, dispassionate, indifferent (to pain/pleasure).

• Other antonym pairs frequently tested: placid vs. fervent, calm vs. passionate, restrained vs. effusive.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The stone was also said to have occult powers.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. intelligible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Occult" means beyond ordinary understanding; mysterious, hidden, or supernatural, i.e., something that cannot be easily understood or explained. (रहस्यमय/गूढ़)

• "Intelligible" means able to be understood; clear and comprehensible, which is the direct opposite of something "occult" (mysterious/beyond understanding). (सुबोध/समझने योग्य)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "latent" (अव्यक्त/छिपा हुआ): Existing but not yet developed or visible — this is close in meaning to "occult" (hidden), not its opposite.

• Option 3: "ambiguous" (अस्पष्ट): Open to more than one interpretation/unclear — this is close in meaning to "occult" (not clearly understood), not its opposite.

• Option 4: "unfathomable" (अगम्य/समझ से परे): Impossible to understand or comprehend fully — this is a near-synonym of "occult", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other meanings of "occult": relating to magic, astrology, or supernatural powers.

• Words meaning "hidden/mysterious": cryptic, esoteric, arcane, enigmatic. Words meaning "clear/understandable": intelligible, lucid, comprehensible, transparent.

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Disintigrate.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "Disintegrate" — to break up or fall apart into small pieces or fragments.
◦ Example: The old newspaper began to disintegrate as soon as it was touched.

• Spelling key: DIS + INTEGRATE. The word is built from the prefix "dis-" (apart/reversal) added to "integrate" (to combine into a whole) — hence the correct middle vowel is "e" (integrate), not "i" (as wrongly printed in "Disintigrate").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Connoisseur" — correctly spelt; a person with expert knowledge/taste in a particular field, e.g., art or food.

• Option 2: "Circumlocution" — correctly spelt; the use of many words where fewer would do, especially to avoid saying something directly.

• Option 3: "Haphazard" — correctly spelt; lacking any obvious organisation or plan; random.

NOTE

• The related noun form is "disintegration" and the opposite is "integrate/integration".

• Other commonly misspelt "dis-" words tested by SSC: dissatisfied, disappear, dissolve, disciple, discipline.

question:
Read the given sentence carefully. Change the meaning of the sentence by replacing the underlined word with its ANTONYM from the following options.
His father warned him not to use vulgar language at home.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. decorous.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Vulgar" means crude, coarse, or lacking in refinement and good taste, especially in language or manners. (अशिष्ट/भद्दा)

• "Decorous" means polite, restrained, and in good taste; showing propriety in behaviour or speech, which is the direct opposite of "vulgar". (शालीन/मर्यादित)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "ribald" (अश्लील): Referring humorously or mockingly to sexual matters; coarse — this is a near-synonym of "vulgar", not its opposite.

• Option 3: "impervious" (अप्रभावित/अभेद्य): Not allowing something to pass through; unaffected by something — unrelated in meaning to "vulgar".

• Option 4: "licentious" (स्वच्छंद/अनैतिक): Promiscuous and unprincipled in sexual matters — this is close to "vulgar" in connotation, not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "vulgar": coarse, crude, uncouth, indecorous, gross.

• Other synonyms of "decorous": proper, dignified, befitting, seemly, genteel.

question:
Select the option that will improve the underlined part of the given sentence.
She's under the allusion that she'll get the job.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. illusion.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Allusion" means an indirect reference to something and is different in meaning from "illusion", which means a false belief or idea; a mistaken impression not based in reality. (भ्रम)

• The fixed expression is "to be under the illusion that...", meaning to wrongly believe something to be true. "Under the allusion" is not idiomatic and confuses two similar-sounding but unrelated words.

• Corrected sentence: "She's under the illusion that she'll get the job."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "hallucination" is incorrect; this refers to perceiving something (seeing/hearing) that is not actually present, usually due to a medical or psychological condition — too strong/specific for this context.

• Option 3: "vision" is incorrect; the fixed idiomatic phrase is "under the illusion", not "under the vision", and "vision" does not carry the sense of a mistaken belief.

• Option 4: "unreality" is incorrect; "under the unreality" is not a standard or idiomatic English expression.

NOTE

• Commonly confused pair: "allusion" (an indirect reference, e.g., "The poem makes an allusion to Greek mythology") vs. "illusion" (a false belief/deceptive appearance).

• Other commonly confused pairs tested by SSC: elusion/illusion, allude/elude, delusion/illusion.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
The common masses have waited for three hours to meet the king in the royal court.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. have been waiting.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The phrase "for three hours" indicates an action that started in the past and has continued up to the present moment — this calls for the Present Perfect Continuous Tense.

• Rule — Present Perfect Continuous Tense: Subject + has/have + been + V1+ing + since/for...

• The subject "the common masses" is plural, so the correct auxiliary is "have", giving "have been waiting".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "has been waiting" is incorrect because "has" is a singular auxiliary, but "the common masses" is a plural subject requiring "have".

• Option 2: "had waiting" is incorrect because "had" must be followed by a past participle (V3) to form the Past Perfect ("had waited"), not the "-ing" form; also, this would wrongly imply the action had ended before another past action.

• Option 4: "will waiting" is incorrect because "will" must be followed by a base verb (V1) or "will be + V1+ing" for future continuous; "will waiting" is not a valid verb form.

NOTE

• Present Perfect Continuous is used with time markers like "for" (duration) and "since" (starting point), e.g., "They have been waiting since morning."

• Do not confuse it with the Present Perfect Simple (has/have + V3), which emphasises completion rather than ongoing duration.

question:
Complete the given sentence with an appropriate homophone from the given options.
There was no one _________ a few of my friends.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. except.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Except" is a preposition meaning "other than" or "excluding", used to exclude something/someone from a general statement.

• The sentence means that nobody was present other than a few friends — this sense is correctly conveyed only by "except": "There was no one except a few of my friends."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "expect" is incorrect; it means to believe something will happen, which does not fit the context of exclusion.

• Option 3: "accept" is incorrect; it means to agree to receive or believe something, which is unrelated to the meaning required here.

• Option 4: "excerpt" is incorrect; it means a short extract from a piece of writing, film, or music, which is completely unrelated to the context.

NOTE

• Commonly confused word group: except (other than) vs. accept (to receive/agree to) vs. expect (to anticipate) vs. excerpt (an extract).

• Memory tip: "Ex-CEPT" is close to "exCLUDE" in meaning — both begin with "ex-" and relate to leaving something out.

question:
Choose an appropriate word that can substitute the bracketed word and complete the sentence meaningfully.
Shelley was very happy (while) I accepted her invitation to her birthday party.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. when.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "While" is used for an action that continues over a period of time and normally introduces a clause in the continuous (progressive) form — it does not fit naturally with the simple past action "I accepted her invitation".

• "When" is used to link two simple past actions that happen closely together in time (the acceptance causing/coinciding with her happiness), which correctly fits here: "Shelley was very happy when I accepted her invitation to her birthday party."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "as" is incorrect here; though "as" can mean "while", it is typically used for two actions happening simultaneously over a duration, not a single completed action causing a reaction.

• Option 3: "after" is incorrect because it would mean Shelley's happiness came only following the acceptance, at a later time, which changes and weakens the intended immediate cause-effect meaning.

• Option 4: "before" is incorrect because it would illogically mean Shelley was happy prior to the invitation being accepted, reversing the intended meaning.

NOTE

• "While" and "as" are generally used with continuous tenses for parallel ongoing actions, e.g., "He called while I was cooking."

• "When" is used with simple tenses for a single point-in-time action or event, e.g., "She smiled when I greeted her."

question:
There is a spelling error in the given sentence. Select the option that contains the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
The choice of buying a yahct was poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. yahct.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "yacht" — a medium-sized sailing or power-driven boat used for racing or pleasure cruising.
◦ Example: They spent the summer sailing their yacht along the coast.

• Spelling key: Y + A + CHT. The letters "ch" come before the final "t", unlike the incorrect order "hct" seen in "yahct". The word is of Dutch origin (from "jacht", meaning "hunt/chase").

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "buying" — correctly spelt; the gerund form of "buy".

• Option 3: "choice" — correctly spelt; a noun meaning an act of selecting between options.

• Option 4: "poor" — correctly spelt; an adjective meaning of low quality or lacking in something.

NOTE

• Other silent-letter/tricky nautical or borrowed-spelling words: yacht, bouquet, silhouette, rendezvous, cologne.

• The "-cht" ending in "yacht" is unusual in English and is frequently tested precisely because of this irregularity.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Absurd
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Irrational.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Absurd" means wildly unreasonable, illogical, or inappropriate; ridiculous. (बेतुका/असंगत)

• "Irrational" means not logical or reasonable; not based on clear thinking, which closely matches the sense of something being absurd/senseless. (अतार्किक)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Sudden" (अचानक): Happening quickly and unexpectedly — refers to timing, not to logic or reasonableness; unrelated to "absurd".

• Option 2: "Arbitrary" (मनमाना): Based on random choice or personal whim rather than any reason or system — different from "absurd", which specifically implies something ridiculous or senseless.

• Option 4: "Abstruse" (दुर्बोध): Difficult to understand; obscure — refers to complexity/difficulty of comprehension, not to something being ridiculous.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "absurd": ridiculous, preposterous, ludicrous, senseless, farcical.

• Do not confuse "absurd" (ridiculous) with "abstruse" (hard to understand) — they are commonly used as distractors for each other in SSC vocabulary questions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the following sentence.
There was some drawing-pins in my desk.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. There are some.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The subject following the introductory "there" is "drawing-pins", which is a plural countable noun.

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "There": when the notional subject after "there" is plural, the verb "be" must also be plural — "There are + plural noun".

• Applying the rule: "There are some drawing-pins in my desk" is the grammatically correct form.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "There is some" is incorrect because "is" is singular and does not agree with the plural noun "drawing-pins".

• Option 2: "There has some" is incorrect because "has" is not used with "there" in this existential construction at all; the verb must be a form of "be", not "have".

• Option 3: "Theirs some" is incorrect because "theirs" is a possessive pronoun and cannot grammatically begin this construction in place of "there".

NOTE

• "There" as an introductory/dummy subject always agrees in number with the noun that follows the verb "be", e.g., "There is a pen" vs. "There are pens".

• Some nouns that look singular but are always treated as plural: scissors, trousers, spectacles, pyjamas — these also take "there are".

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Calm
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Upset.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Calm" means free from excitement, agitation, or disturbance; peaceful and composed in mind. (शांत)

• "Upset" means unhappy, troubled, or disturbed in mind; agitated, which is the direct opposite of being calm and composed. (व्याकुल/परेशान)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Urban" (शहरी): Relating to a town or city — this describes a place, not a state of mind, and is unrelated to "calm".

• Option 2: "Impressed" (प्रभावित): Feeling admiration for someone/something — this describes a positive reaction, not agitation, and is not a true opposite of "calm".

• Option 3: "Quiet" (शांत/खामोश): Making little or no noise; peaceful — this is close in meaning to "calm", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "calm": tranquil, serene, composed, placid, unruffled.

• Other antonyms of "calm": agitated, turbulent, distressed, frantic, perturbed.

question:
Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined part of the given sentence.
Mr. Sengupta's complaint to the higher authority was only a red herring.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. clever bluff.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "a red herring" means something intended to mislead or distract attention from the real issue or question. (ध्यान भटकाने वाली चाल/बहाना)
◦ Example: The defence lawyer's argument was just a red herring to confuse the jury.

• Among the given options, "clever bluff" best captures the sense of a deliberate, misleading deception used to divert attention, matching the idiomatic meaning of "red herring".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "candid confession" (स्पष्ट स्वीकारोक्ति): An honest, open admission of truth — this is the opposite of a misleading tactic like a "red herring".

• Option 2: "fortunate evidence" (सौभाग्यशाली प्रमाण): Genuine, favourable proof — unrelated to the idea of deliberately misleading someone.

• Option 4: "discouraging act" (हतोत्साहित करने वाला कार्य): An act that dampens enthusiasm/hope — this does not capture the specific sense of diversion or deception.

NOTE

• The idiom is believed to originate from using a strong-smelling smoked ("red") herring fish to throw hunting dogs off a scent trail.

• Other idioms of deception/distraction often tested: "to pull the wool over someone's eyes" (to deceive someone), "to beat about the bush" (to avoid getting to the point), "a wild goose chase" (a futile pursuit).

question:
Select the most appropriate word to fill in the blank.
He has __________ vision because of his illness.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. blurred.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Blurred vision" is the standard, fixed medical/everyday collocation used in English to describe an eyesight problem in which things appear unclear or hazy, typically as a symptom of illness.

• The context — "because of his illness" — strongly points to a medical symptom, and "blurred vision" is the natural, idiomatic term used in this sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "unfocused" is incorrect; while it can describe an inability to focus one's eyes, "unfocused vision" is not the standard collocation used for this meaning; "blurred" is preferred.

• Option 3: "obscured" is incorrect; "obscured vision" would suggest something is physically blocking one's view, rather than an internal eyesight impairment caused by illness.

• Option 4: "faded" is incorrect; "faded" describes loss of colour or intensity over time (like a photograph), not an eyesight condition.

NOTE

• Other common illness-related collocations tested by SSC: running nose, high fever, severe headache, chronic pain.

• "Blur/blurred/blurry" can also be used figuratively, e.g., "The line between work and home life has become blurred."
